prompt: A developer hardcodes a third-party API key directly in application source code and commits it to a shared git repository. What is the main security risk?
options: The key becomes part of the repository's history and is visible to anyone with read access (and often CI logs, forks, or backups), even after the file is later deleted
The repository's disk usage will increase noticeably
The linter will fail the build
The build will run slightly slower
optionNotes: Git keeps every committed blob in history, so the key stays recoverable by anyone who can read the repo (or its forks, CI logs, and backups) even after a later deletion; this is the real risk.
A short API key adds a negligible number of bytes to the repository; disk usage is not a security concern here.
Linters check code style and common bugs; most do not detect secrets, and even a lint failure would not be the security risk itself.
Build time is unaffected by the presence of a string literal in source; it is unrelated to the exposure of the secret.
explanation: Once a secret is committed, it persists in git history. Deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from history, so the only reliable fix is to rotate/invalidate the exposed secret and then clean the history.
example:
# gitleaks finds the committed key even after the file was deleted
gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts='--all'
# Finding: AKIA... in config.py at commit 3f2a9c1
# Fix: rotate the key with the provider, then rewrite history
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["Developer hardcodes API key"] --> B["git commit and push"]
    B --> C["Key stored in repo history"]
    C --> D1["Visible to anyone with read access"]
    C --> D2["Leaks via CI logs, forks, backups"]
    E["Later commit deletes file"] -.->|"history still has it"| C
    C --> F["Fix: rotate key, then clean history"]

prompt: If a secret is accidentally committed to git and then removed in a later commit, it is no longer accessible to anyone who has already cloned the repository or who inspects its history.
explanation: Git preserves full history by default. Removing a file in a new commit does not erase it from earlier commits, so the secret remains recoverable. The only dependable remedy is to rotate the exposed secret.
example:
# The secret is still in history even after 'git rm' and a new commit
git log --all -p -S 'AKIA' -- config.py   # shows the commit that added the key
git show 3f2a9c1:config.py                 # prints the old file with the key
# Remedy: rotate the key, then git filter-repo to purge history
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C1["Commit 1: adds secret"] --> C2["Commit 2: removes file"]
    C2 --> C3["Commit 3: HEAD"]
    C1 -.->|"git show or git log -p"| R["Secret still recoverable"]
    R --> X["Removing file does NOT purge history"]
    X --> Y["Rotate the secret immediately"]

prompt: What does the 'principle of least privilege' mean for access control?
options: Every user and service should default to administrator access for convenience
Users and systems should be granted only the minimum permissions needed to perform their tasks, nothing more
Privileges only need to be reviewed once, when an account is created
All applications should share a single, highly privileged service account
optionNotes: Defaulting everyone to administrator maximizes blast radius when any account is compromised; it is the opposite of least privilege.
Granting only the minimum permissions a user or workload needs, and nothing beyond it, is the definition of the principle of least privilege.
Least privilege requires ongoing review because job roles and needs change; a one-time review at account creation lets permissions accumulate over time.
A single shared, highly privileged service account removes attribution and gives every application far more access than it needs.
explanation: Least privilege limits the blast radius if an account, process, or credential is ever compromised, by ensuring it never has more access than its job requires.
diagram:
flowchart TD
    T["Task: read one S3 bucket"] --> Q{"Grant which permissions?"}
    Q -->|"AdministratorAccess"| B["Broad access: huge blast radius if compromised"]
    Q -->|"s3:GetObject on that bucket only"| G["Least privilege: minimum needed"]
    G --> L["Compromise limited to one bucket"]
    G --> R["Review and remove unused rights regularly"]

prompt: What is 'shift-left security' in a DevSecOps context?
options: Delaying every security scan until after production deployment
Relocating the security team to sit closer to the release managers
Moving security testing, reviews, and controls earlier into the development lifecycle instead of only at the end
Moving all responsibility for security onto the operations team
optionNotes: Deferring scans until after production deployment is the extreme of shifting right; issues are found last and cost the most to fix.
Shift-left is about the position of security activities in the delivery timeline, not the physical seating of a security team.
Moving security testing, reviews, and controls earlier in the lifecycle, such as into the IDE, pre-commit hooks, and pull requests, is exactly what shift-left security means.
Shift-left spreads security responsibility across developers and the whole team; it does not hand it all to operations.
explanation: Shift-left means catching issues as early as code is written or reviewed (e.g., in the IDE, pre-commit hooks, or pull requests) rather than only at release time, when defects are far more expensive to fix.
example:
# .pre-commit-config.yaml: run secret and SAST checks before code is even committed
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.18.4
    hooks: [{id: gitleaks}]
  - repo: https://github.com/PyCQA/bandit
    rev: 1.7.9
    hooks: [{id: bandit}]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    I["IDE and pre-commit hooks"] --> P["Pull request: SAST, secret scan"]
    P --> B["Build: SCA, image scan"]
    B --> T["Test and staging: DAST"]
    T --> R["Release and production"]
    S["Shift security LEFT"] -.->|"move checks here"| I
    O["Old way: security only at release"] -.-> R

prompt: Shifting security left generally increases the total cost of fixing vulnerabilities because it requires more tooling earlier in the pipeline.
explanation: Shift-left is intended to reduce overall cost and risk: defects caught during coding or code review are far cheaper and faster to fix than the same defects found in production.
example:
# Same SQL injection bug, different discovery points and cost
# 1. IDE / pre-commit SAST warning  -> fixed in minutes by the author
# 2. Pull request scan              -> fixed before merge
# 3. Production incident            -> outage, forensics, patch, disclosure
# Earlier detection is cheaper, not more expensive
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["Bug found while coding"] -->|"cost 1x"| F["Cheap, fast fix"]
    B["Bug found in code review"] -->|"cost low"| F
    C["Bug found in testing"] -->|"cost higher"| M["Rework, retest"]
    D1["Bug found in production"] -->|"cost highest"| I["Incident, patch, breach risk"]
    S["Shift-left catches bugs earlier"] --> A
    S --> R["Total cost goes DOWN, not up"]

prompt: Which statement best describes SAST (Static Application Security Testing)?
options: It only checks third-party open-source dependencies for known CVEs
It benchmarks application performance under simulated load
It analyzes a running application by sending it crafted HTTP requests, like an external attacker would
It analyzes source code, bytecode, or binaries for vulnerabilities without executing the application
optionNotes: Checking third-party dependencies for known CVEs describes Software Composition Analysis (SCA), not SAST.
Benchmarking under simulated load is performance or load testing, which is not a security testing technique at all.
Sending crafted HTTP requests to a running application is Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST), the black-box counterpart of SAST.
Analyzing source code, bytecode, or binaries for vulnerabilities without executing the program is precisely what SAST does.
explanation: SAST is a 'white-box' technique: it inspects the application's own code or compiled artifacts directly, without running the application, to find issues like injection flaws or insecure patterns.
example:
# Semgrep scans source code without running the application
semgrep --config p/owasp-top-ten src/
# src/db.py:42  python.lang.security.audit.formatted-sql-query
#   Detected string formatting in a SQL query (possible injection)
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S["Source code, bytecode, binaries"] --> T["SAST scanner"]
    T --> N["No execution needed: white-box"]
    T --> F1["SQL injection pattern"]
    T --> F2["Insecure API usage"]
    T --> F3["Hardcoded secret"]
    F1 --> R["Findings in IDE or CI"]
    F2 --> R
    F3 --> R

prompt: Which statement best describes DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing)?
options: It tests a running instance of the application from the outside, similarly to how an attacker would probe it, without needing access to source code
It signs container images so their provenance can be verified
It reviews source code line by line before the application is compiled or built
It generates a Software Bill of Materials listing every dependency
optionNotes: Probing a deployed, running application from the outside without source access is the defining characteristic of DAST.
Signing container images to verify provenance is the job of tools like `cosign`, not a testing technique.
Reviewing source code before compilation describes SAST, the static, white-box approach.
Generating a Software Bill of Materials is done by SBOM tools such as `syft`, not by DAST.
explanation: DAST is a 'black-box' technique that exercises a deployed, running application (e.g., a web app) and observes its behavior and responses to find exploitable vulnerabilities.
example:
# OWASP ZAP baseline scan probes a running staging site from the outside
docker run --rm -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable \
  zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.com -r zap-report.html
# WARN: Missing Anti-clickjacking Header [10020] x 12
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as "DAST scanner"
    participant A as "Running application"
    Note over D: black-box, no source code needed
    D->>A: Crawl pages and endpoints
    D->>A: Send malicious payloads (XSS, SQLi)
    A-->>D: Observe responses and behavior
    D->>D: Report exploitable vulnerabilities

prompt: What is the primary purpose of Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tools?
options: To encrypt data at rest in a database
To identify known vulnerabilities and license issues in third-party and open-source dependencies used by an application
To measure the percentage of code covered by unit tests
To automatically reformat source code to a consistent style
optionNotes: Encrypting data at rest is handled by database or storage-layer encryption features, not by SCA tools.
Inventorying open-source and third-party dependencies and flagging known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and license problems is the core purpose of SCA.
Measuring unit test coverage is done by coverage tools such as `coverage.py` or `istanbul`, which have no security focus.
Reformatting code to a consistent style is the job of formatters like `prettier` or `black`, not of SCA.
explanation: SCA tools inventory the open-source and third-party components an application depends on and flag ones with known vulnerabilities (CVEs) or problematic licenses.
example:
# Audit third-party dependencies for known CVEs and license issues
npm audit --audit-level=high
# or, for any ecosystem:
trivy fs --scanners vuln,license --severity HIGH,CRITICAL .
diagram:
flowchart LR
    M["Manifest: package.json, go.mod, pom.xml"] --> S["SCA tool"]
    S --> I["Inventory of third-party components"]
    I --> V["Vulnerability DB: known CVEs"]
    I --> L["License check: GPL, AGPL risk"]
    V --> R["Report: upgrade lodash 4.17.15"]
    L --> R
    N["Custom business logic"] -.->|"NOT covered by SCA"| S

prompt: Which of the following statements about SAST, DAST, and SCA are correct?
options: SAST can be run without deploying or executing the application
DAST requires a running instance of the application to test
SCA primarily analyzes an application's own custom business logic for design flaws
SCA helps detect known vulnerable versions of open-source libraries
DAST can only be performed by reading source code, never against a running service
optionNotes: SAST inspects code or compiled artifacts directly, so it needs no deployed or running instance of the application.
DAST sends real requests to a live application and observes its responses, so a running instance is required.
SCA looks at third-party and open-source components, not at an application's own custom business logic; design flaws there are found by SAST, manual review, or threat modeling.
Matching the versions of open-source libraries in use against vulnerability databases is the main job of SCA.
DAST is a black-box technique that works against a running service and does not need source code at all, so this claim reverses how DAST works.
explanation: SAST works on source/binaries without running the app; DAST needs a live, running target; SCA focuses on third-party/open-source dependency risk (known CVEs and licenses), not custom business logic — that distinction is exactly what SCA does not cover.
example:
# Typical CI stages using all three techniques
sast:  semgrep --config auto src/           # static, no runtime needed
sca:   trivy fs --scanners vuln .           # known CVEs in dependencies
dast:  zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.com   # needs a live target
diagram:
flowchart TD
    Q{"What are you scanning?"} -->|"Your own code, not running"| SAST["SAST: static analysis, no deploy needed"]
    Q -->|"A live running app from outside"| DAST["DAST: requires running instance"]
    Q -->|"Third-party dependencies"| SCA["SCA: known CVEs in open-source libs"]
    SAST --> C["Complementary layers, use all three"]
    DAST --> C
    SCA --> C

prompt: What does the acronym `SBOM` — a formal inventory of the components, libraries, and dependencies that make up a piece of software — stand for?
explanation: An SBOM lists every component in a software artifact, similar to an ingredient list, so consumers can identify what they're running and check it against vulnerability databases.
example:
# Generate an SBOM for a container image and list its components
syft packages nginx:1.27 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
jq '.components[] | "\(.name)@\(.version)"' sbom.json | head
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["Software artifact"] --> S["SBOM: Software Bill of Materials"]
    S --> C1["Component: openssl 3.0.2"]
    S --> C2["Component: log4j 2.14.1"]
    S --> C3["Component: alpine base 3.18"]
    C2 --> V["Match against vulnerability DB"]
    V --> R["Log4Shell affected: act now"]

prompt: Which of the following are widely used standard formats for representing a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)?
options: CycloneDX
SPDX
Dockerfile
OpenAPI
SWID
optionNotes: CycloneDX is an OWASP-originated SBOM standard with JSON and XML representations, widely used by security tooling.
SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange) is a Linux Foundation and ISO standard for SBOMs and license data.
A Dockerfile is a build recipe for container images; it describes build steps, not an inventory of installed components.
OpenAPI is a specification for describing HTTP APIs and their endpoints, not a software component inventory.
SWID (Software Identification) tags are an ISO/IEC 19770-2 format that NTIA recognizes as an SBOM format alongside SPDX and CycloneDX.
explanation: CycloneDX, SPDX, and SWID (Software Identification tags) are recognized SBOM formats. A Dockerfile builds container images and an OpenAPI document describes an HTTP API — neither is an SBOM format.
example:
# syft can emit an SBOM in the two most common formats
syft packages ./app -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json
syft packages ./app -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.cdx.json
# grype can then scan either SBOM for known CVEs
grype sbom:sbom.spdx.json
diagram:
flowchart TD
    S["SBOM standard formats"] --> A["CycloneDX (OWASP)"]
    S --> B["SPDX (Linux Foundation, ISO)"]
    S --> C["SWID tags (ISO/IEC 19770-2)"]
    N["Not SBOM formats"] --> D1["Dockerfile: builds images"]
    N --> D2["OpenAPI: describes HTTP APIs"]

prompt: What is the main purpose of scanning a container image before it is deployed?
options: To reduce the on-disk size of the image
To automatically generate Kubernetes manifests for the image
To detect known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in the OS packages and libraries baked into the image
To improve the container's startup time
optionNotes: Reducing image size is done through slim base images and multi-stage builds; a vulnerability scan does not shrink the image.
Scanners do not emit Kubernetes manifests; tools like Helm or Kustomize generate those.
Comparing the OS packages and libraries inside each image layer against vulnerability databases to surface known CVEs is the purpose of image scanning.
Startup time depends on image size and application initialization; scanning has no effect on it.
explanation: Image scanners inspect the layers of a container image and compare installed packages and libraries against vulnerability databases, surfacing known CVEs before the image ever runs.
example:
# Scan an image for known CVEs before pushing or deploying it
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:1.4.2
# Fails the pipeline if any HIGH or CRITICAL vulnerability is found
diagram:
flowchart LR
    B["Build container image"] --> S["Image scanner (Trivy, Grype)"]
    S --> L["Inspect each layer"]
    L --> P["OS packages and app libraries"]
    P --> V["Compare with CVE databases"]
    V -->|"critical CVE found"| F["Fail pipeline, fix base image"]
    V -->|"clean"| D1["Push and deploy"]

prompt: What does the `cosign` tool, part of the Sigstore project, primarily do?
options: It generates Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` objects from traffic captures
It scans container images for outdated OS packages
It compiles a Dockerfile into an OCI-compliant image
It signs and verifies container images and other software artifacts, optionally without needing to manage long-lived private keys
optionNotes: Generating `NetworkPolicy` objects from traffic captures is something tools like Cilium's editor or `netfetch` attempt; it is unrelated to cosign.
Scanning images for outdated packages is the domain of vulnerability scanners such as Trivy or Grype, not cosign.
Compiling a Dockerfile into an OCI image is done by `docker build`, `buildah`, or `kaniko`; cosign works on images after they are built.
Signing and verifying container images and other artifacts, including keyless signing bound to an OIDC identity, is exactly what cosign does.
explanation: cosign lets teams sign artifacts (like container images) and later verify those signatures, giving consumers assurance about who published an artifact and that it hasn't been tampered with. It supports 'keyless' signing tied to an OIDC identity.
example:
# Keyless signing: cosign uses your OIDC identity, no long-lived key
cosign sign ghcr.io/acme/app@sha256:9f2e...
# Verify before deploying
cosign verify ghcr.io/acme/app@sha256:9f2e... \
  --certificate-identity=ci@acme.dev \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as "Publisher"
    participant C as "cosign"
    participant R as "Registry"
    participant V as "Consumer"
    P->>C: cosign sign image@sha256
    C->>R: Store signature next to image
    V->>C: cosign verify image
    C->>R: Fetch signature
    C-->>V: Verified: who published it, untampered

prompt: Which of the following are components of the Sigstore project's keyless-signing ecosystem?
options: Fulcio — a certificate authority that issues short-lived certificates tied to an OIDC identity
Rekor — a public transparency log that records signing events
cosign — the CLI used to sign and verify artifacts
kube-bench — a CIS Kubernetes benchmark scanner
Terraform — an infrastructure-as-code provisioning tool
optionNotes: Fulcio is Sigstore's certificate authority; it exchanges an OIDC token for a short-lived code-signing certificate, which is the foundation of keyless signing.
Rekor is Sigstore's append-only public transparency log that records signatures and attestations so they can be audited later.
cosign is the Sigstore CLI that performs signing and verification of images and other artifacts, using Fulcio and Rekor in keyless mode.
kube-bench audits a Kubernetes cluster against the CIS benchmark; it is a hardening checker, not part of Sigstore.
Terraform is HashiCorp's infrastructure-as-code tool for provisioning cloud resources and has nothing to do with artifact signing.
explanation: Fulcio, Rekor, and cosign together make up Sigstore's keyless signing flow: Fulcio issues a short-lived cert bound to an OIDC identity, cosign uses it to sign, and Rekor timestamps the signing event in a public, tamper-evident log. kube-bench and Terraform are unrelated tools.
example:
# Keyless flow behind 'cosign sign':
# 1. cosign gets an OIDC token (e.g. from GitHub Actions)
# 2. Fulcio issues a short-lived signing certificate for that identity
# 3. cosign signs the artifact and uploads the signature
# 4. Rekor records the signing event in its transparency log
rekor-cli search --artifact app.tar.gz   # look up entries later
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as "cosign CLI"
    participant O as "OIDC provider"
    participant F as "Fulcio CA"
    participant R as "Rekor log"
    U->>O: Authenticate (GitHub, Google)
    O-->>U: OIDC identity token
    U->>F: Request cert for identity
    F-->>U: Short-lived signing certificate
    U->>U: Sign artifact, key discarded
    U->>R: Record signature in transparency log
    R-->>U: Timestamped, tamper-evident entry

prompt: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) provenance attestations are primarily intended to help answer which question about a software artifact?
options: How the artifact was built, from what source, and by which build system — i.e., build integrity
Which team should be billed for the artifact's cloud usage
Which known CVEs affect the artifact's dependencies
How much memory the artifact consumes at runtime
optionNotes: Provenance records which source, build steps, and builder produced an artifact, letting consumers verify build integrity; this is the question SLSA is designed to answer.
Cost allocation and billing are handled by cloud tagging and FinOps tooling, not by provenance attestations.
Listing known CVEs in dependencies is the job of SBOMs and SCA scanners, a separate supply-chain concern from build integrity.
Runtime memory consumption is observed with monitoring and profiling tools; it has nothing to do with how the artifact was built.
explanation: SLSA focuses on the integrity of the build process itself — proving what source and build steps produced an artifact and that it wasn't tampered with — which is a different concern from SBOM/SCA (what components are inside) or runtime monitoring.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S["Source repo at commit abc123"] --> B["Build system: GitHub Actions"]
    B --> A["Artifact: image digest"]
    B --> P["SLSA provenance attestation"]
    P --> Q1["Which source?"]
    P --> Q2["Which builder?"]
    P --> Q3["Was the build tampered with?"]
    V["Consumer verifies build integrity"] --> P
    N["SBOM answers: what is inside"] -.->|"different concern"| P

prompt: What is the OWASP Top 10?
options: A certification exam required for penetration testers
A regularly updated awareness document that ranks the most critical security risks to web applications
A built-in Kubernetes admission controller
A list of the ten most popular JavaScript frameworks
optionNotes: The OWASP Top 10 is freely available awareness material, not a certification exam; pentester certifications include OSCP and GPEN.
A periodically updated, community-driven awareness document that ranks the most critical web application risk categories is what the OWASP Top 10 is.
Kubernetes admission controllers are components of the API server such as `PodSecurity` or `ValidatingAdmissionWebhook`; OWASP Top 10 is unrelated to them.
The document ranks security risk categories, not JavaScript frameworks or any other popularity list.
explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is a broadly referenced awareness document, periodically updated by the OWASP community, that highlights the categories of risk considered most critical for web applications at the time of publication.
example:
# OWASP Top 10 (2021) category IDs, often used to label scanner rules
# A01 Broken Access Control    A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components
# A02 Cryptographic Failures   A07 Identification and Auth Failures
# A03 Injection                A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures
# A05 Security Misconfiguration A10 SSRF
semgrep --config p/owasp-top-ten src/
diagram:
flowchart LR
    O["OWASP community"] --> T["OWASP Top 10 awareness document"]
    T --> U["Updated periodically: 2017, 2021"]
    T --> R["Ranks most critical web app risk categories"]
    R --> C1["Broken Access Control"]
    R --> C2["Injection"]
    R --> C3["Security Misconfiguration"]
    T -.->|"not a certification or law"| X["Guidance, not a standard body"]

prompt: In the OWASP Top 10 (2021 edition), which category covers flaws such as SQL injection and OS command injection, where untrusted input is interpreted as part of a command or query?
options: Cryptographic Failures
Server-Side Request Forgery
Injection
Security Misconfiguration
optionNotes: Cryptographic Failures (A02) covers weak or missing encryption and poor key management, not interpreter abuse via untrusted input.
Server-Side Request Forgery (A10) is when an attacker makes the server issue requests to unintended destinations; it is not about commands or queries being altered.
Injection (A03) is the category for SQL, OS command, LDAP, and similar flaws where untrusted data is interpreted as part of a command or query.
Security Misconfiguration (A05) covers insecure defaults, open cloud storage, verbose errors, and similar setup problems, not injection.
explanation: Injection covers cases where untrusted data is sent to an interpreter (SQL, OS shell, LDAP, etc.) as part of a command or query, letting an attacker alter its intended behavior.
example:
# Injection-safe query: parameters are bound, never concatenated
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))
# Unsafe pattern that SAST flags:
# cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'")
diagram:
flowchart LR
    U["Untrusted input: name' OR 1=1 --"] --> A["Application builds query by concatenation"]
    A --> I["Interpreter: SQL, OS shell, LDAP"]
    I --> X["Command meaning altered by attacker"]
    O["OWASP category: Injection"] -.-> X
    F["Fix: parameterized queries, input validation"] --> I

prompt: In the OWASP Top 10 (2021 edition), what does the 'Broken Access Control' category refer to?
options: Sending verbose stack traces to end users in error pages
Using outdated TLS cipher suites in a web server
Storing passwords with a fast, unsalted hash
Failures that let users act outside their intended permissions, such as viewing another user's data or bypassing authorization checks
optionNotes: Leaking stack traces to users is an information-disclosure issue typically classed under Security Misconfiguration.
Outdated TLS cipher suites fall under Cryptographic Failures, since they weaken encryption of data in transit.
Fast, unsalted password hashing is a Cryptographic Failures problem related to insecure credential storage.
Letting users act outside their intended permissions, such as viewing another user's records or bypassing authorization checks, is what Broken Access Control (A01) describes.
explanation: Broken Access Control covers enforcement failures around what an authenticated user is actually allowed to do or see, letting them escalate privileges or access resources they shouldn't.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    U["User A, logged in"] --> R["GET /orders/1234 (belongs to User B)"]
    R --> C{"Authorization check?"}
    C -->|"missing or flawed"| B["Broken Access Control: User A sees B's data"]
    C -->|"enforced"| D1["403 Forbidden"]
    B --> E["Also: privilege escalation, bypassing role checks"]

prompt: What does TLS (Transport Layer Security) primarily provide for data sent over a network?
options: Encryption, integrity checking, and authentication of the communicating parties
Automatic load balancing across backend servers
Compression of HTTP response bodies only
Faster DNS resolution for the destination host
optionNotes: Confidentiality through encryption, integrity through MACs or AEAD, and authentication of at least the server via certificates are the three core guarantees TLS provides.
Load balancing is done by load balancers and reverse proxies; TLS can be terminated there, but it does not distribute traffic itself.
TLS does not compress HTTP bodies; HTTP-level compression (gzip, brotli) is separate, and TLS-level compression was removed because of the CRIME attack.
DNS resolution happens before the TLS connection begins and is not accelerated by TLS; DNS-over-TLS protects DNS queries but is a different protocol.
explanation: TLS protects data in transit by encrypting it (confidentiality), detecting tampering (integrity), and typically authenticating at least the server via its certificate.
example:
# Inspect the TLS handshake: certificate (authentication) and negotiated cipher
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E 'Protocol|Cipher|subject='
# Protocol  : TLSv1.3
# Cipher    : TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"TLS session"| S["Server"]
    T["TLS provides"] --> E["Confidentiality: data encrypted"]
    T --> I["Integrity: tampering detected via MAC"]
    T --> A["Authentication: server cert verified"]
    E --> P["Protects data in transit"]
    I --> P
    A --> P

prompt: A typical TLS connection uses asymmetric cryptography during the handshake (for authentication and key exchange) and then switches to a symmetric cipher, such as AES, to encrypt the bulk of the session's data.
explanation: Asymmetric operations are computationally expensive, so TLS uses them briefly to authenticate the server and establish a shared session key, then relies on fast symmetric encryption for the actual data transfer — a hybrid approach.
example:
# TLS 1.3 handshake in brief
# 1. ClientHello / ServerHello: ECDHE key exchange (asymmetric)
# 2. Server certificate + signature: authenticates the server (asymmetric)
# 3. Both sides derive the session key
# 4. Application data encrypted with a symmetric AEAD cipher
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 | grep Cipher
# Cipher: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as "Client"
    participant S as "Server"
    Note over C,S: Handshake: asymmetric (slow, used briefly)
    C->>S: ClientHello, key share
    S-->>C: Certificate, key share, signature
    C->>C: Verify cert, derive shared session key
    Note over C,S: Data transfer: symmetric AES (fast)
    C->>S: Encrypted application data
    S-->>C: Encrypted application data

prompt: What is the key property that distinguishes hashing from encryption?
options: Encryption is only ever used to protect passwords
Hashing is a one-way function that cannot feasibly be reversed to recover the original input, while encryption is designed to be reversible with the correct key
Hashing requires a secret key to compute, just like encryption
Hashing always produces output the same length as its input
optionNotes: Encryption is used for data at rest, data in transit, backups, and much more; and passwords should be hashed rather than encrypted.
A cryptographic hash is a one-way digest that cannot feasibly be inverted, whereas encryption is designed to be reversed with the right key; that is the key distinction.
Plain hashes such as SHA-256 need no secret key; a keyed variant (HMAC) exists, but hashing in general is unkeyed, unlike encryption.
Hash functions produce a fixed-length digest regardless of input size, for example 256 bits for SHA-256.
explanation: A cryptographic hash is a one-way digest — you cannot feasibly recover the input from it. Encryption is deliberately reversible: anyone holding the correct key can decrypt the ciphertext back to plaintext.
example:
# Hashing: one-way digest, no key, cannot be reversed
sha256sum app.tar.gz          # verify integrity of a download
# Encryption: reversible with the key
age -r age1abc... -o secrets.env.age secrets.env
age -d -i key.txt secrets.env.age > secrets.env
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P1["password123"] -->|"SHA-256"| H["Hash: ef92b7..."]
    H -.->|"one-way, cannot reverse"| X["No way back to input"]
    P2["Plaintext"] -->|"encrypt with key"| C["Ciphertext"]
    C -->|"decrypt with key"| P3["Plaintext recovered"]
    H --> U1["Use: integrity, password storage"]
    C --> U2["Use: confidentiality"]

prompt: Base64 encoding provides meaningful confidentiality for sensitive data, comparable to encryption.
explanation: Base64 is a reversible encoding scheme for representing binary data as text. It uses no secret key, and anyone can decode it instantly, so it provides no confidentiality at all — it is not a substitute for encryption.
example:
# Base64 is trivially reversible, so it hides nothing
echo -n 'password123' | base64      # cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=
echo 'cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=' | base64 -d # password123
# Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded; enable encryption at rest separately
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S["secret: hunter2"] -->|"base64 encode"| E["c2VjcmV0OiBodW50ZXIy"]
    E -->|"base64 -d, no key needed"| S2["secret: hunter2"]
    E --> N["No secret key: anyone can decode"]
    N --> X["Encoding is NOT encryption"]
    P["Plaintext"] -->|"AES with secret key"| C["Ciphertext: needs key to read"]

prompt: In symmetric encryption, how many distinct keys are used to encrypt and then decrypt the same data?
options: A new, unrelated key for every byte of data
No key is required at all
One shared key is used for both encrypting and decrypting
Two independent keys: one public, one private
optionNotes: Using a fresh unrelated key for every byte describes a one-time pad, which is impractical and not how symmetric ciphers like AES operate.
Every cipher requires a key; keyless transformations such as base64 are encodings, not encryption.
Symmetric algorithms such as AES and ChaCha20 use a single shared secret key for both encryption and decryption.
A public/private key pair is the hallmark of asymmetric cryptography such as RSA or ECDSA, not symmetric encryption.
explanation: Symmetric algorithms like AES use a single shared secret key for both encryption and decryption, which makes them fast but requires securely distributing that key to every party who needs it.
example:
# AES-256-GCM: the same key encrypts and decrypts
openssl rand -hex 32 > aes.key
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -in db.sql -out db.sql.enc -pass file:aes.key
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -in db.sql.enc -out db.sql -pass file:aes.key
diagram:
flowchart LR
    K["ONE shared secret key"] --> E["Encrypt"]
    K --> D1["Decrypt"]
    P["Plaintext"] --> E
    E --> C["Ciphertext"]
    C --> D1
    D1 --> P2["Plaintext"]
    K -.->|"challenge"| S["Key must be securely shared with every party"]

prompt: Which of these is an example of an asymmetric (public-key) cryptographic algorithm?
options: bcrypt
AES
ChaCha20
RSA
optionNotes: bcrypt is a deliberately slow password-hashing function based on Blowfish; it is not an encryption algorithm at all.
AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric block cipher that uses one shared key for encryption and decryption.
ChaCha20 is a symmetric stream cipher, usually paired with Poly1305 for authenticated encryption; it does not use a key pair.
RSA uses a mathematically linked public/private key pair for encryption and digital signatures, making it an asymmetric algorithm.
explanation: RSA uses a mathematically linked public/private key pair — one key encrypts or verifies, the other decrypts or signs. AES and ChaCha20 are symmetric ciphers, and bcrypt is a password-hashing function, not an encryption algorithm.
example:
# Generate an RSA key pair: private key stays secret, public key is shared
openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:4096 -out private.pem
openssl pkey -in private.pem -pubout -out public.pem
# Sign with the private key, verify with the public key
openssl dgst -sha256 -sign private.pem -out release.sig release.tar.gz
diagram:
flowchart TD
    A["Asymmetric: public/private key pair"] --> RSA["RSA"]
    A --> ECC["ECDSA, Ed25519"]
    S["Symmetric: one shared key"] --> AES["AES"]
    S --> CC["ChaCha20"]
    H["Password hashing, not encryption"] --> B["bcrypt"]
    RSA --> U["Public key encrypts or verifies, private key decrypts or signs"]

prompt: Which practice is essential for securely managing SSH keys?
options: Keeping your private key secret at all times and only ever distributing the matching public key to servers
Committing your private key to a shared git repository so the team can back it up
Reusing one passphrase-less private key across every server and every teammate
Emailing your private key to teammates so they can log in as you when you're on leave
optionNotes: Keeping the private key secret and distributing only the public key to servers is the whole basis of SSH public-key authentication.
Committing a private key to a repository exposes it to everyone with repo access and to git history forever; backups should use an encrypted password manager or vault.
Reusing a single passphrase-less key across all servers and people means one leak compromises everything and removes any audit trail.
Sending a private key by email exposes it in transit and in mailboxes and lets others impersonate you; delegated access should be granted with the colleague's own key.
explanation: SSH's security model depends on the private key never leaving your control. Only the public key should ever be placed on remote servers (in `authorized_keys`); sharing or exposing the private key breaks the whole trust model.
example:
# Generate a passphrase-protected key pair, install only the public half
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'alice@laptop'
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519            # private key: owner-only
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub alice@server.example.com
# ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server now holds the public key only
diagram:
flowchart LR
    G["ssh-keygen"] --> PRIV["Private key: id_ed25519"]
    G --> PUB["Public key: id_ed25519.pub"]
    PRIV --> L["Stays on your machine only, passphrase-protected"]
    PUB --> S["Copied to server ~/.ssh/authorized_keys"]
    S --> A["Server challenges, private key proves identity"]
    PRIV -.->|"never share, email, or commit"| X["Trust model broken if exposed"]

prompt: Best practice is for each individual user to have their own personal SSH key pair, rather than an entire team sharing a single private key.
explanation: Individual key pairs preserve an audit trail (each login is attributable to one person) and let you revoke a single compromised or departed user's access without having to rotate credentials for the whole team.
example:
# One key per person; revoke a single user without touching anyone else
# /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3...alice alice@laptop
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3...bob   bob@laptop
# Alice leaves: delete only her line, Bob keeps working
sed -i '/alice@laptop/d' /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys
diagram:
flowchart TD
    T["Shared team key"] --> T1["Login not attributable to a person"]
    T --> T2["One person leaves: rotate for everyone"]
    I["Individual key pair per user"] --> I1["Audit trail: each login maps to one person"]
    I --> I2["Revoke one key without affecting others"]
    I --> I3["Least privilege per user"]

prompt: What is multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
options: Logging in from several devices at the same time
Requiring two or more independent forms of evidence from different factor categories — such as a password plus a one-time code — to verify identity
Changing your password several times throughout the year
Requiring an unusually long single password
optionNotes: Logging in from several devices simultaneously concerns session management and has nothing to do with proving identity with multiple factors.
Requiring two or more independent factors from different categories, such as a password plus a one-time code, is the definition of MFA.
Changing a password frequently is a rotation policy; it is still a single knowledge factor.
A very long password is still one factor (something you know); length strengthens it but does not make it multi-factor.
explanation: MFA combines evidence from at least two distinct categories (something you know, have, or are) so that compromising just one factor, like a password, is not enough to authenticate as the user.
example:
# Enable MFA for the AWS CLI: password (know) + TOTP code (have)
aws iam enable-mfa-device --user-name alice \
  --serial-number arn:aws:iam::123456789012:mfa/alice \
  --authentication-code1 123456 --authentication-code2 789012
# Sessions now require: aws sts get-session-token --serial-number ... --token-code 654321
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as "User"
    participant S as "Service"
    U->>S: Username and password (something you know)
    S-->>U: Prompt for second factor
    U->>S: One-time code from authenticator (something you have)
    S->>S: Both factors valid?
    S-->>U: Access granted
    Note over U,S: Stolen password alone is not enough

prompt: Which of the following are recognized categories of authentication factors used in MFA?
options: Something you know (e.g., a password or PIN)
Something you have (e.g., a hardware token or authenticator app)
Something you are (e.g., a fingerprint or other biometric)
Something you bought (e.g., the price of your laptop)
Somewhere you registered an email address
optionNotes: Knowledge factors such as passwords, PINs, and security answers make up the 'something you know' category.
Possession factors such as hardware security keys, smart cards, and authenticator apps make up the 'something you have' category.
Inherence factors such as fingerprints, face, or iris scans make up the 'something you are' category.
Purchase price of a device is not evidence of identity and is not a recognized authentication factor category.
Having registered an email address is an account attribute, not a factor category; an emailed code is a weak form of possession, but registration itself proves nothing.
explanation: The three classic authentication factor categories are knowledge ('something you know'), possession ('something you have'), and inherence ('something you are'). Using factors from two or more different categories is what makes authentication multi-factor.
example:
# A typical MFA login combines two categories:
#   password        -> something you know
#   TOTP / YubiKey  -> something you have
#   fingerprint     -> something you are
# WebAuthn (FIDO2) registers a hardware authenticator as the possession factor
navigator.credentials.create({ publicKey: { ... } })
diagram:
flowchart TD
    M["MFA: two or more DIFFERENT categories"] --> K["Something you KNOW: password, PIN"]
    M --> H["Something you HAVE: hardware token, authenticator app"]
    M --> A["Something you ARE: fingerprint, face"]
    K --> E1["Password + OTP app = MFA"]
    H --> E1
    K --> E2["Password + security question = same category, not MFA"]

prompt: Why is regularly rotating credentials such as API keys and database passwords considered good practice?
options: It makes credentials easier for humans to memorize
It is required syntax in most programming languages
It limits the window of time during which a leaked or stolen credential remains useful to an attacker
It removes the need for any access control checks
optionNotes: Rotation produces new random values regularly, which makes credentials harder, not easier, for humans to memorize; they should live in a secrets manager.
No programming language has syntax that requires rotating credentials; rotation is an operational security practice.
Regular rotation bounds how long a leaked or stolen credential remains valid, limiting the damage an attacker can do with it.
Rotation does not replace authorization; access control checks are still needed for every request.
explanation: Even with strong safeguards, credentials can leak. Rotating them regularly (and immediately after suspected compromise) shrinks the amount of time a stolen credential stays valid and useful.
example:
# Rotate a database password automatically with AWS Secrets Manager
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id prod/db/app \
  --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:rotate \
  --rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30
# A leaked password is useful to an attacker for at most 30 days
diagram:
flowchart LR
    L["Credential leaks at day 3"] --> W1["No rotation: usable for years"]
    L --> W2["Rotate every 30 days: usable until day 30"]
    L --> W3["Rotate on suspicion: usable minutes"]
    W1 --> R["Rotation shrinks the window an attacker can use it"]
    W2 --> R
    W3 --> R

prompt: If you strongly suspect a credential, such as a cloud API key, has been exposed, you should rotate it immediately rather than waiting for its next scheduled rotation.
explanation: Waiting for a scheduled rotation leaves a known-exposed credential usable by an attacker in the meantime. Suspected compromise should always trigger immediate rotation and, where possible, revocation of the old credential.
example:
# Key spotted in a public repo: revoke and replace right now, not next month
aws iam create-access-key --user-name ci-deployer       # issue replacement
# update the secret in the pipeline, then:
aws iam update-access-key --user-name ci-deployer --access-key-id AKIAOLD... --status Inactive
aws iam delete-access-key --user-name ci-deployer --access-key-id AKIAOLD...
diagram:
flowchart TD
    S["Suspect API key exposed"] --> Q{"Wait for scheduled rotation?"}
    Q -->|"No: rotate now"| N["Issue new key, revoke old one"]
    N --> A["Attacker's copy is useless"]
    Q -->|"Yes: wait until next month"| W["Old key valid for weeks"]
    W --> B["Attacker uses it in the meantime"]
    N --> L["Then investigate logs for misuse"]

prompt: What is the primary purpose of HashiCorp Vault?
options: It is a CI/CD pipeline execution engine
It is an authoritative DNS server
It is a container orchestration platform, similar to Kubernetes
It centrally stores and controls access to secrets, and can dynamically generate short-lived credentials such as database passwords or API keys
optionNotes: CI/CD execution engines are tools like Jenkins, GitLab CI, or GitHub Actions; Vault is often called from pipelines but does not run them.
Authoritative DNS is served by software like BIND, CoreDNS, or Route 53, not by Vault.
Container orchestration is Kubernetes' role; Vault integrates with Kubernetes for auth and secret injection but does not schedule containers.
Centralized secrets storage with access policies, encryption as a service, and dynamic short-lived credentials is the primary purpose of HashiCorp Vault.
explanation: Vault provides centralized secrets storage, fine-grained access control, encryption as a service, and the ability to generate dynamic, short-lived credentials on demand instead of relying on long-lived static secrets.
example:
# Vault issues a short-lived Postgres credential on demand
vault read database/creds/app-readonly
# Key             Value
# lease_id        database/creds/app-readonly/abc123
# lease_duration  1h
# username        v-token-app-read-x7k2
# password        A1b2-...   (revoked automatically after 1h)
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["App or CI job"] -->|"authenticate"| V["HashiCorp Vault"]
    V --> S["Central secrets storage (KV)"]
    V --> P["Policies: fine-grained access control"]
    V --> D1["Dynamic secrets engine"]
    V --> E["Encryption as a service (transit)"]
    D1 -->|"short-lived DB creds"| DB["Database"]
    A -.->|"no static secrets in config"| S

prompt: In Vault, credentials that are generated on demand for a specific request, tied to a lease, and automatically revoked once that lease expires, are known by what two-word term?
explanation: Dynamic secrets are created fresh for each consumer and have a limited lifetime (lease), so there is no long-lived static credential sitting around waiting to be leaked.
example:
# Configure a dynamic-secrets role: every read creates a fresh, leased DB user
vault write database/roles/app-readonly \
  db_name=postgres \
  creation_statements="CREATE ROLE \"{{name}}\" WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '{{password}}' VALID UNTIL '{{expiration}}'; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO \"{{name}}\";" \
  default_ttl=1h max_ttl=24h
diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Requested: app asks Vault for DB access
    Requested --> Generated: Vault creates unique user and password
    Generated --> Active: lease TTL 1h starts
    Active --> Renewed: app renews before expiry
    Renewed --> Active
    Active --> Revoked: lease expires or is revoked
    Revoked --> [*]: Vault deletes DB user

prompt: What does RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) allow Kubernetes administrators to do?
options: Define roles that bundle sets of permissions, and bind those roles to users, groups, or service accounts
Automatically scale pods based on CPU usage
Encrypt all traffic between pods on the cluster network
Schedule pods onto specific nodes based on labels
optionNotes: Defining `Role`/`ClusterRole` objects that bundle verbs on resources and binding them to users, groups, or service accounts through `RoleBinding`/`ClusterRoleBinding` is what Kubernetes RBAC does.
Scaling pods on CPU usage is the job of the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, not RBAC.
Encrypting pod-to-pod traffic is provided by a service mesh (mTLS) or a CNI such as Cilium with WireGuard, not by RBAC.
Placing pods on labeled nodes uses `nodeSelector`, node affinity, or taints and tolerations; RBAC controls API access, not scheduling.
explanation: Kubernetes RBAC lets you define `Role`/`ClusterRole` objects describing allowed actions on resources, then grant them to subjects via `RoleBinding`/`ClusterRoleBinding`, enabling least-privilege access to the API server.
example:
# Role bundles permissions; RoleBinding grants it to a ServiceAccount
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: pod-reader, namespace: dev}
rules:
- {apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]}
# kubectl create rolebinding ci-pod-reader --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=dev:ci -n dev
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["Role: pod-reader"] --> P["Rules: get, list pods in namespace dev"]
    RB["RoleBinding"] --> R
    RB --> S1["User: alice"]
    RB --> S2["Group: developers"]
    RB --> S3["ServiceAccount: ci-bot"]
    S1 -->|"kubectl get pods -n dev"| API["API server allows"]
    S1 -.->|"kubectl delete pods"| DEN["API server denies"]

prompt: Kubernetes Pod Security Standards define three policy levels. Which level is the most restrictive, enforcing current pod hardening best practices such as running as a non-root user?
options: Baseline
Restricted
Permissive
Privileged
optionNotes: Baseline is the middle level; it blocks known privilege escalations such as privileged containers and host namespaces but still allows root users.
Restricted is the most locked-down level, requiring non-root execution, dropped capabilities, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and a seccomp profile.
Permissive is not one of the Pod Security Standards levels; the three defined levels are Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted.
Privileged is the least restrictive level, allowing essentially anything and intended for trusted system workloads.
explanation: The three Pod Security Standards levels are Privileged (unrestricted), Baseline (blocks known privilege escalations), and Restricted (the most locked-down, following current hardening best practices like non-root execution and dropped capabilities).
example:
# Enforce the restricted profile on a namespace via the built-in PodSecurity admission
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: payments
  labels: {pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted}
# Pods running as root or with extra capabilities are now rejected
diagram:
flowchart TD
    PSS["Pod Security Standards"] --> P["Privileged: unrestricted, no policy"]
    PSS --> B["Baseline: blocks known privilege escalations"]
    PSS --> R["Restricted: most locked-down"]
    R --> R1["runAsNonRoot"]
    R --> R2["drop ALL capabilities"]
    R --> R3["no privilege escalation"]
    B -->|"stricter"| R

prompt: By default, if no `NetworkPolicy` objects are defined in a Kubernetes cluster, all pods can communicate with all other pods without restriction.
explanation: Kubernetes pod networking is flat and permissive by default. NetworkPolicy resources are additive and restrictive: once a policy selects a pod, that pod becomes default-deny for the traffic types the policy governs, assuming the CNI plugin enforces NetworkPolicy.
example:
# Turn the default allow-all into default-deny for a namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny-all, namespace: payments}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
# Requires a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, etc.)
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["Pod A (ns: frontend)"] <-->|"allowed by default"| B["Pod B (ns: backend)"]
    B <-->|"allowed by default"| C["Pod C (ns: db)"]
    N["Apply NetworkPolicy selecting Pod C"] --> D1["Pod C: default-deny for governed traffic"]
    D1 --> E["Only whitelisted sources reach C"]
    N -.->|"needs CNI that enforces policy"| CNI["Calico, Cilium"]

prompt: Setting `securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` on a Kubernetes pod or container does what?
options: It automatically patches any known vulnerabilities in the container image
It grants the container additional Linux capabilities it would not otherwise have
It causes the container to fail to start if it is configured to run as the root user (UID 0), reducing the impact of a potential container breakout
It encrypts the container's root filesystem at rest
optionNotes: Patching image vulnerabilities requires rebuilding the image with updated packages; no securityContext field does that.
Adding Linux capabilities is done with `securityContext.capabilities.add`; `runAsNonRoot` restricts rather than grants.
With `runAsNonRoot: true` the kubelet validates the effective UID and refuses to start a container that would run as UID 0, limiting damage from a breakout.
Filesystem encryption at rest is a node or storage-class concern (for example encrypted EBS volumes); it is not controlled by `runAsNonRoot`.
explanation: `runAsNonRoot` is a guardrail: Kubernetes refuses to start the container if it would run as UID 0, so that even if an attacker escapes the application, they don't land with root privileges inside the container.
example:
# Kubelet refuses to start this container if the image runs as UID 0
containers:
- name: app
  image: ghcr.io/acme/app:1.4.2
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001   # explicit non-root UID so the check can pass
diagram:
flowchart TD
    P["Pod spec: runAsNonRoot: true"] --> K["Kubelet checks container user"]
    K -->|"UID 0 (root)"| F["Container refuses to start: CreateContainerConfigError"]
    K -->|"UID 1000"| S["Container starts"]
    S --> B["Attacker escapes app: no root inside container"]
    F --> X["Fix: set runAsUser or USER in Dockerfile"]

prompt: What does setting `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` achieve for a container?
options: It makes the resulting container image smaller on disk
It disables all network access for the container
It automatically provisions a persistent volume for the pod
It prevents the container's root filesystem from being written to at runtime, making it harder for an attacker to tamper with binaries or drop malware
optionNotes: Image size is fixed at build time; a runtime mount flag does not change the bytes on disk or in the registry.
Network access is governed by `NetworkPolicy` and the CNI; `readOnlyRootFilesystem` has no effect on networking.
Persistent volumes are provisioned through `PersistentVolumeClaim` objects and storage classes, not through this security setting.
Mounting the container root filesystem read-only prevents a compromised process from writing files or modifying binaries, which is the hardening goal of this setting.
explanation: With a read-only root filesystem, an attacker who compromises the running process can't write new files or modify existing ones on the container's filesystem; any directory the app legitimately needs to write to should be mounted as a separate writable volume.
example:
# Immutable root filesystem plus an explicit writable scratch volume
containers:
- name: app
  securityContext: {readOnlyRootFilesystem: true}
  volumeMounts: [{name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}]
volumes:
- {name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["Container with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true"] --> RF["Root filesystem: read-only"]
    A["Attacker compromises process"] -->|"write malware to /usr/bin"| RF
    RF --> D1["Write denied"]
    C --> V["emptyDir volume mounted at /tmp"]
    APP["App writes cache"] --> V
    V --> OK["Writable, isolated from binaries"]

prompt: Which of the following `securityContext` settings help harden a Kubernetes pod in line with the 'restricted' Pod Security Standard?
options: `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`
`capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`
`privileged: true`
`runAsNonRoot: true`
`hostNetwork: true`
optionNotes: Setting `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` sets the no_new_privs flag so a process cannot gain more privileges than its parent (for example via setuid binaries); the restricted profile requires it.

Dropping all Linux capabilities with `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` removes kernel privileges the workload does not need and is required by the restricted profile (only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` may be added back).
A privileged container gets nearly all host capabilities and device access, effectively equal to root on the node; every Pod Security Standard except Privileged forbids it.
Requiring a non-root UID with `runAsNonRoot: true` is one of the restricted profile's mandatory controls.
Sharing the host's network namespace via `hostNetwork: true` exposes host interfaces and bypasses NetworkPolicy; it is forbidden even at the Baseline level.
explanation: Disallowing privilege escalation, dropping all Linux capabilities by default, and forcing non-root execution are core hardening controls. `privileged: true` and `hostNetwork: true` do the opposite — they widen the container's access to the host.
example:
# securityContext that satisfies the 'restricted' Pod Security Standard
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
diagram:
flowchart TD
    R["Restricted PSS hardening"] --> A["allowPrivilegeEscalation: false"]
    R --> B["capabilities.drop: ALL"]
    R --> C["runAsNonRoot: true"]
    W["Widens host access instead"] --> D1["privileged: true"]
    W --> E["hostNetwork: true"]
    A --> S["Smaller blast radius on breakout"]
    B --> S
    C --> S

prompt: What does the acronym `CVE`, used to uniquely identify a publicly disclosed security vulnerability (for example, CVE-2021-44228), stand for?
explanation: CVE provides a standardized identifier and description for a publicly known vulnerability, so different tools, vendors, and researchers can all refer to the same issue unambiguously.
example:
# Look up a CVE and check whether an image is affected
trivy image --severity CRITICAL log4j-demo:1.0
# CVE-2021-44228  log4j-core  2.14.1  fixed in 2.15.0  (Log4Shell)
curl -s https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2021-44228 | jq '.vulnerabilities[0].cve.descriptions[0].value'
diagram:
flowchart LR
    V["Vulnerability discovered in openssl"] --> N["CNA assigns CVE-2024-3094"]
    N --> ID["Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures identifier"]
    ID --> T1["Scanner: Trivy"]
    ID --> T2["Vendor advisory"]
    ID --> T3["NVD entry with CVSS score"]
    T1 --> S["Everyone refers to the same issue unambiguously"]
    T2 --> S
    T3 --> S

prompt: The CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) base score falls within which numeric range?
options: 0 to 5
optionNotes: CVSS base scores run from 0.0 to 10.0, with 9.0 and above mapped to the Critical band.
A 1 to 100 range resembles the EPSS percentage or some vendor risk scores, but it is not the CVSS scale.

A 0 to 5 range is not CVSS; it resembles star ratings or some internal risk matrices.

# CVSS v3.1 base score from a vector string
# CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H  -> 10.0 (Critical)
# Qualitative bands: None 0.0 | Low 0.1-3.9 | Medium 4.0-6.9 | High 7.0-8.9 | Critical 9.0-10.0
grype myapp:1.4.2 --fail-on high   # gate on the severity band

    S --> L["0.1 to 3.9: Low"]
    S --> M["4.0 to 6.9: Medium"]

prompt: Which principle best summarizes the 'zero trust' security model?
options: Rely solely on a strong perimeter firewall to keep attackers out
Never trust, always verify: every request must be authenticated and authorized based on identity and context, regardless of where it originates
Trust is granted permanently to a user once they complete MFA at login
Trust any device or user automatically once they are inside the corporate network perimeter
optionNotes: Relying on a perimeter firewall alone is the castle-and-moat model that zero trust was created to replace.
'Never trust, always verify' with explicit authentication and authorization of every request based on identity and context, regardless of network location, is the core of zero trust.
Zero trust favors continuous, per-request evaluation; a permanent grant after a single MFA prompt contradicts that.
Automatically trusting anything inside the corporate network is exactly the implicit, location-based trust that zero trust rejects.
explanation: Zero trust replaces implicit, location-based trust (e.g., 'inside the network = safe') with continuous, explicit verification of identity, device posture, and authorization for every request.
example:
# Istio AuthorizationPolicy: every call must present a verified identity, even inside the mesh
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata: {name: orders-allow, namespace: shop}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: orders}}
  rules:
  - from: [{source: {principals: ["cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/checkout"]}}]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["Every request, any origin"] --> V["Verify identity (user, workload)"]
    V --> D1["Check device posture and context"]
    D1 --> A["Authorize for this specific resource"]
    A -->|"pass"| G["Grant least-privilege access"]
    A -->|"fail"| X["Deny"]
    Z["Zero trust: never trust, always verify"] -.-> R
    O["Old model: inside network = trusted"] -.->|"rejected"| Z

prompt: A zero trust architecture assumes that traffic originating from inside the corporate network is inherently more trustworthy than traffic from outside it.
explanation: Zero trust explicitly rejects trust based on network location. Internal traffic must be authenticated and authorized just like external traffic — there is no automatically trusted 'inside'.
example:
# Zero trust: internal service calls still need mTLS identity and authorization
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata: {name: default, namespace: shop}
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT   # plaintext 'internal' traffic is rejected
diagram:
flowchart TD
    E["External request"] --> V["Authenticate and authorize"]
    I["Internal request (corporate LAN, VPN)"] --> V
    V -->|"verified"| A["Access granted"]
    V -->|"not verified"| D1["Denied"]
    N["Network location grants NO implicit trust"] -.-> I
    L["Lateral movement after one breach is contained"] -.-> V

prompt: What is the primary function of a Web Application Firewall (WAF)?
options: It encrypts database backups before they are stored
It manages an organization's DNS records
It monitors and filters HTTP/HTTPS traffic to a web application to block common attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting
It compiles application source code for deployment
optionNotes: Encrypting backups is done by the backup tooling or storage service with KMS keys; a WAF never touches stored data.
DNS records are managed by DNS services such as Route 53 or Cloud DNS, which are separate from web application firewalls.
Inspecting HTTP(S) requests in front of a web application and blocking those matching attack patterns such as SQL injection or XSS is the primary function of a WAF.
Compiling source code is a build-system task; a WAF operates on live traffic, not on code.
explanation: A WAF sits in front of a web application and inspects incoming HTTP(S) requests, blocking or flagging traffic that matches known attack patterns before it ever reaches the application.
example:
# Attach the AWS managed Core Rule Set (blocks common SQLi/XSS patterns) to an ALB
aws wafv2 create-web-acl --name app-waf --scope REGIONAL --default-action Allow={} \
  --rules file://crs-rule.json   # ManagedRuleGroupStatement: AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet
aws wafv2 associate-web-acl --web-acl-arn $ACL_ARN --resource-arn $ALB_ARN
# Blocked requests show up as action=BLOCK in the WAF logs

    U["Legitimate user request"] --> W["WAF: inspects HTTP/HTTPS"]
    A["Attacker: ' OR 1=1 or script tag payload"] --> W
    W -->|"matches SQLi or XSS rule"| B["Blocked or flagged"]
    W -->|"clean"| APP["Web application"]
    W -.->|"layer 7 only, not network firewall"| N["Does not replace a network firewall"]

prompt: What best describes a Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack?
options: An attacker forging a digital signature to trust a malicious container image
An attacker repeatedly guessing a single user's password
An attacker exploiting a SQL injection flaw to read data out of a database
Traffic generated from many distributed sources overwhelms a target's resources or bandwidth so legitimate users can no longer access it
optionNotes: Forging a signature to get a malicious image trusted is a supply-chain integrity attack, not a denial of service.
Repeated password guessing against one account is a brute-force or credential-stuffing attack.
Reading data through a SQL injection flaw is an injection attack aimed at confidentiality, not availability.
Overwhelming a target's bandwidth or resources with traffic from many distributed sources so legitimate users are locked out is the definition of a DDoS attack.
explanation: DDoS attacks flood a target with traffic from numerous distributed sources simultaneously, exhausting network bandwidth, connection limits, or application resources so real users can't get through.
example:
# Symptom of a volumetric DDoS in nginx access logs: huge request volume from many IPs
awk '{print $1}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
# Mitigation: rate limit per client
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m rate=10r/s;

flowchart LR
    B1["Botnet host 1"] --> T["Target server"]
    B2["Botnet host 2"] --> T
    B3["Botnet host N (thousands)"] --> T
    T --> E["Bandwidth, connections, CPU exhausted"]
    E --> X["Legitimate user cannot connect"]
    U["Legitimate user"] -.->|"timeout"| T

prompt: Which of the following help mitigate the impact of a DDoS attack?
options: Rate limiting requests per client
Traffic scrubbing services or an anycast CDN that absorbs and filters traffic
Autoscaling backend capacity to absorb traffic spikes
Disabling TLS to reduce server processing overhead
Removing all firewalls to maximize throughput
optionNotes: Per-client rate limiting caps how many requests any one source can make, blunting application-layer floods and abusive clients.
Anycast CDNs and scrubbing centers spread and filter attack traffic across many global points of presence before it reaches the origin.
Autoscaling adds backend capacity during a surge, helping the service stay available while other controls filter the flood.
Disabling TLS would expose users to interception and does not stop a volumetric flood; TLS termination at the edge is the standard approach.
Removing firewalls eliminates a filtering layer and would let more attack traffic through, worsening rather than mitigating the attack.
explanation: Rate limiting, scrubbing/CDN absorption, and autoscaling all help a service withstand or deflect a flood of traffic. Disabling TLS or removing firewalls would weaken security without meaningfully helping against volumetric attacks.
example:
# Layered DDoS mitigation
# 1. Edge: anycast CDN / scrubbing (Cloudflare, AWS Shield Advanced) absorbs volumetric floods
# 2. Per-client rate limiting at the proxy
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m rate=20r/s;
# 3. Autoscale the backend to ride out what gets through
kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=3 --max=30 --cpu-percent=60
diagram:
flowchart LR
    F["DDoS flood"] --> C["Anycast CDN or scrubbing service absorbs and filters"]
    C --> R["Rate limiting per client"]
    R --> S["Autoscaled backend absorbs remaining spikes"]
    S --> A["Service stays available"]
    X["Not mitigations: disable TLS, remove firewall"] -.->|"weakens security"| F

prompt: What is the main purpose of audit logging in a production system?

To automatically remediate discovered vulnerabilities
To reduce cloud storage costs
To improve application response times
optionNotes: Recording who performed which action on which resource and when, to support accountability, incident forensics, and compliance evidence, is the purpose of audit logging.
Audit logs are a record, not a remediation engine; fixing vulnerabilities requires patching or configuration changes.
Audit logs add storage volume and usually cost money to retain; they do not reduce cloud storage costs.
Writing audit events adds a small overhead; it never speeds up application responses.
explanation: Audit logs create a tamper-evident record of security-relevant events (logins, permission changes, data access, etc.), which is essential for investigating incidents and demonstrating compliance.

kind: Policy
rules:
- level: RequestResponse

  - {group: "", resources: ["secrets"]}
  - {group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io, resources: ["rolebindings", "clusterrolebindings"]}

    L --> W["Who: alice"]

    L --> T["When: timestamp"]
    L --> U1["Incident forensics"]

prompt: Which of the following statements about compliance frameworks are correct?

An audit shows that defined controls were in place at a point in time; it cannot prove the absence of vulnerabilities in code.

HIPAA concerns health information privacy (not Kubernetes), and no compliance certification can guarantee zero vulnerabilities.

prompt: Why should application passwords never be stored in plaintext in a database?
options: Plaintext values take up noticeably more disk space
If the database is ever breached, plaintext passwords are immediately usable by an attacker to access accounts — and, due to password reuse, potentially other services too
Plaintext passwords cannot be checked against a login form
Most databases technically cannot store text values
optionNotes: Password strings are tiny; disk usage is irrelevant to the decision, and hashes are often longer than the plaintext anyway.
A breach of a plaintext password table gives the attacker every account instantly, and reused passwords let them pivot to other services; that is why plaintext storage is unacceptable.
Plaintext passwords can trivially be compared to a login form value; the problem is that they should not exist to be compared.
Databases store text perfectly well; the constraint is a security requirement, not a technical limitation.
explanation: Storing passwords in plaintext means a single database breach instantly compromises every user's credentials, with no additional work required by the attacker.
example:
# Store only a salted, slow hash; verify by re-hashing the login attempt
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher()
stored = ph.hash("correct horse battery staple")   # $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$...
ph.verify(stored, login_attempt)   # raises on mismatch
diagram:
flowchart LR
    DB["Database breach"] --> P["Plaintext passwords"]
    P --> A1["Instant account takeover, no cracking needed"]
    P --> A2["Password reuse: other services compromised too"]
    DB --> H["Salted slow hashes (bcrypt, Argon2)"]
    H --> S["Attacker must brute-force each hash slowly"]

prompt: Why are bcrypt and Argon2 preferred over a single fast round of SHA-256 for storing user passwords?
options: They do not require any salt to be secure
They produce a shorter digest than SHA-256
They are deliberately slow and tunable (a configurable work factor) and are designed to be used with a per-user salt, which makes large-scale brute-force and rainbow-table attacks far more expensive
They run faster than SHA-256, so logins feel snappier
optionNotes: Salts are still essential with bcrypt and Argon2; both generate and embed a per-user salt automatically rather than eliminating the need for one.
Digest length is not the point; a bcrypt string is 60 characters and Argon2 output is configurable, and neither shortness nor length improves password security by itself.
A tunable, intentionally slow work factor plus per-user salts is what makes bcrypt and Argon2 resistant to large-scale brute force and rainbow tables, and is why they are preferred.
They are intentionally slower than SHA-256; the small login delay is the price of making offline cracking expensive.
explanation: General-purpose hashes like SHA-256 are built to be fast, which is exactly the wrong property for password storage — it lets attackers try billions of guesses per second. bcrypt and Argon2 are intentionally slow and configurable, and are used with salts to defeat precomputed rainbow tables.
example:
# bcrypt cost factor makes each guess deliberately slow (~250 ms at cost 12)
import bcrypt
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12))
# $2b$12$<22-char salt><31-char hash>  -- salt is embedded, per user
bcrypt.checkpw(attempt.encode(), hashed)
diagram:
flowchart LR
    F["Fast hash: SHA-256"] --> B["Billions of guesses per second on GPU"]
    B --> C["Passwords cracked quickly"]
    S["bcrypt or Argon2"] --> W["Tunable work factor: deliberately slow"]
    S --> SA["Per-user salt"]
    W --> D1["Brute force very expensive"]
    SA --> R["Rainbow tables useless"]

prompt: Which password-hashing algorithm won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition and, in its Argon2id variant, is now widely recommended for storing passwords?
explanation: Argon2 (particularly the Argon2id variant) is the modern, competition-vetted choice for password hashing, alongside longstanding options like bcrypt and scrypt.
example:
# Argon2id with OWASP-recommended minimum parameters
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=2, memory_cost=19456, parallelism=1)  # 19 MiB
print(ph.hash("s3cret"))
# $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$...
